title: Operator-chain launch overheads: attention micro-profiling
content:
Purpose:
This is a focused, experimental scratchpad documenting micro-profiling we ran to isolate operator-chaining and kernel-launch overheads in attention implementations. Goal: determine whether end-to-end token latency regressions at small batch sizes (1-4) are caused by compute inefficiency inside FlashAttention/paged kernels or by host-side overheads (launchs, copies, syncs, allocator).

Background / motivation:
- Several customer workloads report ~10-30% higher median token latency when switching from a fused attention path (op-fused kernels) to FlashAttention variants on A100/P4d.
- Previous notes (attention-kernels-exploration-notes) covered algorithmic correctness and throughput; this doc focuses on micro-latency when sequence length is short (<=384) and batch small.
- Hypothesis: kernel launch overhead + multiple small kernels (op-chaining) and CPU->GPU memcpy + stream synchronization dominate at low batch sizes.

Environment (baseline):
- Instance: a100-80gb (p4d-ish timings replicated on A100-SXM2)
- CUDA: 12.2, cuDNN: 9.6, NCCL: 2.17
- PyTorch: 2.2.1 + Triton 2.0.0 + flash-attention v2.0.0 (internal build)
- Serving runtime build: main@2026-01-15 with op-fusion toggles behind feature flags
- Workload: causal LM, 16-heads, 32k vocab, model shape tested: 1) 6B (config small), 2) 13B (wider KV cache)
- Kernel configs tested: fused-op chain (single fused attention op), FlashAttention (single kernel per attention but non-fused surrounding ops), paged-attn (paging KV to flash-backed tensor layout), and a handcrafted micro-op-chaining variant (split into 3 kernels: qk matmul, softmax+scale, out matmul)

Test methodology:
- Microbench harness in Python that runs 1000 steps warmup + 2000 measured iterations; collects per-token latency using CUDA events (elapsed time on GPU) and host-side timestamp (time.monotonic) to capture host enqueue overhead.
- Nsight Compute (ncu) sampling on short runs (200 iters) for kernel launch times and kernel durations.
- nvprof-style trace (cudaProfilerStart/Stop) for one sample to inspect memcpy calls.
- Profiling variants: single-stream vs multiple streams, pinned vs non-pinned host buffers, caching allocator enabled/disabled, cudamallocAsync on/off.

Key observations (raw):
- End-to-end median token latency (13B model, seq=128, batch=1):
  - fused-op: 18.6 ms (gpu-event), host-observed 22.1 ms
  - flash-attn: 22.9 ms (gpu-event), host-observed 28.4 ms
  - paged-attn: 24.8 ms (gpu-event), host-observed 30.6 ms
  - handcrafted 3-kernel: 26.3 ms (gpu-event), host 32.2 ms

- Kernel launch breakdown (ncu sampling, averaged across iterations):
  - fused-op: 1 kernel, kernel_time=16.8 ms, launch_overhead negligible (0.2 ms total)
  - flash-attn: 3 kernels (precompute reorders + core flash + post-reorder), kernel_time sum=19.1 ms, inter-kernel gaps total=2.6 ms
  - paged-attn: 4 kernels (page-checks + page-copy + core + postprocess), kernel_time sum=20.1 ms, inter-kernel gaps=3.7 ms
  - handcrafted: kernels similar to flash-attn but without reorder optimizations; inter-kernel gaps=4.9 ms

- Host-side observations from tracing:
  - Several small cudaMemcpyAsync calls from CPU->GPU in paged-attn path when page-miss occurs; these appear as host enqueue spikes (~1.2–2.5 ms each) and cause blocking on subsequent stream waits.
  - With pinned host buffers, host enqueue overhead drops by ~0.6 ms across the board, but overall gap still significant for multi-kernel paths.
  - Using multiple CUDA streams to overlap page copies with compute provided benefit only when batch>=4; for batch=1 it increased scheduling jitter and made tail latency worse.

Memory allocator effects:
- With caching allocator (default), occasional spikes correlate with cudaMalloc calls in paged path when we see new page allocations; enabling pre-allocation (reserved workspace) eliminated those spiky outliers but did not change median by more than 5%.
- cudamallocAsync reduced host enqueue overhead slightly for inter-kernel allocations but required synchronized fallback on older runtimes; consider enabling when available.

Quantitative micro-table (median times in ms):
- columns: path | seq=64 b=1 | seq=128 b=1 | seq=128 b=4
- fused-op | 10.4 | 18.6 | 12.8
- flash-attn | 12.7 | 22.9 | 14.2
- paged-attn | 13.6 | 24.8 | 16.9
- handcrafted | 14.1 | 26.3 | 17.6

Interpreting the numbers:
- Pure compute time (sum of kernel durations) is similar between fused and flash, often flash slightly higher due to reorders, but the bulk of the observed delta for small batches is in inter-kernel gaps and host enqueue times.
- Fused-op single kernel avoids kernel launch overheads and avoids intermediate host/GPU syncs and reorder copies, which explains its consistently lower p50 at small batch sizes.
- Paged-attn adds complexity: page-miss handling adds CPU->GPU copies that are not overlapped effectively at batch=1 leading to visible penalties.

Hypotheses tested and quick experiments:
1) Overhead mainly due to kernel-launch/stream-synchronization: verified by re-running flash-attn with a synthetic aggregator kernel that fuses post-reorder work — reduced inter-kernel gaps by ~1.6ms and moved median closer to fused-op.
2) Host allocation spikes: mitigated via pre-reserving workspace and enabling cudamallocAsync where supported; smoothed tails but little median improvement.
3) Pinned buffers and single hot-stream: reduced enqueue latency but harmed concurrency for batch>1. Conclusion: keep pinned buffers only for low-batch hot paths via flag.

Recommendations / next steps:
- Short-term (2–3 sprint):
  - Add a small-batch opt-in path in the runtime that enables fused-attention-style single-kernel for seq<=128 & batch<=2 for selected models. (Ticket JIRA-INF-1123)
  - For paged-attn, implement a small-page prefetcher that issues copies earlier on a background stream when we see pattern predicts page usage; experiment with a 16-token lookahead prefetch.
  - Add a runtime flag to force pinned host buffers on low-batch interactive routes; measure cost on throughput tests.

- Medium-term (quarter):
  - Work with FlashAttention upstream to explore reduced-reorder kernels (one-shot kernels that accept packed QKV) and reduced intermediate memcopies.
  - Implement a lightweight micro-kernel aggregator in Triton that can optionally combine reorder+softmax+matmul into a single launch when shapes allow.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How general is the fused-op advantage across model shapes (e.g., 8k context)? Preliminary tests show fused still wins at short seqs, but for long seq the fusion sometimes regresses due to memory pressure.
- Can we design a generalizable prefetcher that doesn't blow up memory when many concurrent requests cause many prefetched pages? Need capacity model.
- Interaction with quantized kernels (4-bit) is untested fully; do fused kernels play nicely with quantized matmuls?

Short checklist for reproducibility (commands):
- Run python microbench/attn_latency.py --model 13B --seq 128 --batch 1 --impl flashattn --warmup 1000 --iters 2000 --trace ncu
- Nsight compute sampling: ncu --target-processes all --launch-skip 100 --sample 200 --set full microbench_case.collect
- To reproduce paged-attn page-miss: use random kv-pages pattern seed 42: python microbench/attn_latency.py --impl paged --page-seed 42 --page-miss-rate 0.15

Action items assigned:
- Kira: implement small-batch feature flag and run p50/p99 sweep across internal model zoo (deadline: 2026-03-01).
- Maya: prototype page-prefetch background worker and run memory-capacity analysis (deadline: 2026-03-15).
- Rafael: open PR to add pinned-buffer toggle to runtime and run perf comparisons on p4d fleet (PR: linked artifact).

Notes-to-self / friction log:
- Nsight output noisy with caching allocator; set PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 for cleaner traces when measuring allocations.
- Triton kernel codegen bug triggered on CUDA 12.2 with certain block configs — worked around by forcing older code-path for small-M.

References and prior docs:
- attention-kernels-exploration-notes (overview of algorithms)
- attention-opfusion-profiling-playbook (older runbook with general profiling steps)
- GH PR #427 (runtime pinned-buffer flag prototype)

Status: working draft with concrete microbench numbers. Goal is to converge on a runtime-level mitigation for interactive low-batch latencies without regressing throughput on batch workloads. Please add comments or push PRs against the branch perf/opchain-experiments.
